wiki.art.families.julep-family.tips: SILVER CUP: traditional and functional — conducts the cold from the ice. If you don't have one, use a highball with plenty of crushed ice. CRUSHED ICE: essential (not cubes) — creates the surface that frosts. Buy an ice crusher or pound with a Lewis bag. MINT: do NOT muddle aggressively — just press gently to release the oils, never tear the leaves (they release bitter chlorophyll). The mint bouquet garnish goes near the straw — so you smell the mint with every sip. Use bourbon at 45-50% ABV minimum (the crushed ice dilutes a lot).
wiki.art.families.punch-family.sub: Bowl cocktails — the oldest social tradition
wiki.art.families.punch-family.descripti: Punch is the MOTHER OF ALL COCKTAILS — the oldest family in bartending, originating in the 17th century before the term "cocktail" even existed. It is prepared in a large bowl for sharing, with five classic components: spirit (strong), citrus (sour), sugar (sweet), water (weak), and spices (tea/bitters). The traditional rhyming rule: "One of sour, two of sweet, three of strong, four of weak." It is the father of the modern cocktail — all Sours and Highballs derive from Punch structure.
wiki.art.families.punch-family.examples: PLANTER'S PUNCH (dark rum, lime, syrup, bitters, water — the Jamaican classic). PHILADELPHIA FISH HOUSE PUNCH (rum, cognac, peach, lemon, tea — since 1732). REGENT'S PUNCH (champagne, rum, green tea, citrus, pineapple — 1820s, favorite of King George IV). CHATHAM ARTILLERY PUNCH (bourbon, cognac, rum, champagne, tea, lemon — brutal, "the most deadly drink ever devised"). CHRISTMAS BOWL (mulled wine, brandy, orange, spices). BAJAN RUM PUNCH (Mount Gay rum, lime, syrup, Angostura, nutmeg — traditional Barbados recipe).
wiki.art.families.punch-family.origin: British colonial India, 1600s. The word "punch" derives from Hindi "pāñc" or Sanskrit "pañca" (five) — for its five ingredients. British sailors of the East India Company took it back to England and from there to the world. 1632: first written mention in an English document. 17th-19th centuries: the golden age of Punch — it was THE way to drink socially, served from bowls in taverns and homes. The modern individual cocktail emerges as a "mini-punch" in the mid-19th century.
wiki.art.families.punch-family.structure: CLASSIC FORMULA (the rhymed recipe): "1 sour, 2 sweet, 3 strong, 4 weak" — 1 part citrus, 2 parts sweet, 3 parts spirit, 4 parts "weak" (tea, water, champagne). Spices at the end (cinnamon, clove, nutmeg, bitters). For a 10-person bowl: 250ml citrus + 500ml sugar/syrup + 750ml spirit + 1000ml tea/water. Large ice block in the center (chills without fast dilution). Abundant garnish: citrus slices, berries, whole spices floating.
wiki.art.families.punch-family.tips: LARGE ICE BLOCK: freeze water in a big container (Tupperware, bundt pan) 24h ahead — melts 5x slower than small cubes. Add to the bowl just before serving. MAKE SPICED SYRUPS: strong black tea, spice infusions, super juice for higher yield. Punch is EXCELLENT for events — prepare a batch and guests serve themselves (less work for the bartender). Always taste before serving — adjust acid/sweet. A well-made Punch bowl is more impressive than 10 individual cocktails.
wiki.art.families.tiki-family.sub: Complex tropical cocktails — the Polynesian fantasy
wiki.art.families.tiki-family.descriptio: Tiki is an aesthetic and cultural cocktail category created in California in the 1930s that imagined an exotic Polynesian fantasy. Tiki cocktails are complex — often with 5-10 ingredients — blending multiple rums, citrus, spiced syrups (falernum, orgeat), fruit liqueurs, and bitters. Served in dramatic vessels (tiki mugs, coconuts, hollowed pineapples) with excessive tropical garnishes. It was the most popular bar style of the 1940s-1960s, disappeared, and returned with force in the 2000s.
wiki.art.families.tiki-family.examples: MAI TAI (aged rum, dark rum, lime, orgeat, curaçao — Trader Vic 1944). ZOMBIE (3 rums, falernum, lime, grapefruit, grenadine, absinthe, Angostura, allspice dram — Don 1934). SCORPION (rum, brandy, lime, orange, orgeat). NAVY GROG (3 rums, lime, grapefruit, honey, soda). PAINKILLER (rum, coconut, pineapple, orange, nutmeg). JUNGLE BIRD (dark rum, Campari, pineapple, lime). THREE DOTS AND A DASH (rhum agricole, falernum, lime, orange, honey, Angostura, allspice dram). SATURN (gin, falernum, orgeat, lime, passion fruit). BLUE HAWAII, MISSIONARY'S DOWNFALL, HURRICANE, SUFFERING BASTARD.
wiki.art.families.tiki-family.origin: California, USA. 1933: Ernest Raymond Beaumont-Gantt opens "Don the Beachcomber" in Hollywood after the end of Prohibition — the first tiki bar. 1937: Victor Bergeron opens "Trader Vic's" in Oakland. These two men created most of the classic tiki cocktails — and fiercely rivaled each other, guarding recipes as trade secrets. 1944: Trader Vic creates the Mai Tai. 1960s: tiki cultural explosion driven by Polynesian films, the Pacific War, and Californian leisure culture. 1970s: decline. 2000s: revival led by bartenders like Jeff Berry (Beachbum).
wiki.art.families.tiki-family.structure: There is NO simple formula — each tiki cocktail is unique. Common principles: MULTIPLE RUMS (white + dark + overproof + agricole), 2-3 CITRUS JUICES (lime, grapefruit, orange), SPICED SYRUP (falernum, orgeat, honey, cinnamon), FRUIT LIQUEUR (maraschino, curaçao, crème de menthe), BITTERS (Angostura, pimento dram), SOMETIMES ABSINTHE. Technique: vigorous shake with crushed ice, serve over more crushed ice in a tiki mug or exotic glass. Abundant garnish: mint, lime, cherries, parasols, flamed cinnamon spray. Each cocktail tells a story.
wiki.art.families.tiki-family.tips: MULTIPLE RUMS: the key to tiki. Minimum stock: white rum (Bacardí/Plantation 3 Stars), Jamaican dark (Smith & Cross, Appleton), Demerara (El Dorado 5yo), overproof (Wray & Nephew 63%). Homemade FALERNUM AND ORGEAT are notably better than commercial. TIKI MUGS: not a gimmick — they insulate cold better and create the theatrical experience. GENEROUS GARNISH: mint, tropical fruits, parasols, edible flowers. Jeff "Beachbum" Berry's books are the modern tiki bible. A good tiki bar is a full experience — aromas, visuals, rituals.
wiki.art.beer.cerveza.sub: The most-consumed fermented drink in the world
wiki.art.beer.cerveza.description: Beer is the oldest and most-consumed alcoholic drink in the world — 190 billion liters a year. Made from cereals (mainly malted barley), water, hops, and yeast, it ranges from light lagers to dense, opaque stouts. For a professional bartender, knowing beer styles is essential: beer cocktails (Michelada, Shandy, Snakebite), pairings, and beer as the highest-grossing category in any bar.
wiki.art.beer.cerveza.history: 4000 BC: first evidence of beer in Sumer. 3000 BC: Egypt produces beer on an industrial scale. 6th century: European monks master the craft. 1516: Reinheitsgebot in Bavaria. 1842: Josef Groll creates the first Pilsner in Plzeň (Czechia) — the golden lager that would conquer the world is born. 1876: Pasteur discovers yeast — a revolution in quality control. 20th century: macro-breweries dominate. 1980s-present: the craft beer revolution restores diversity.
wiki.art.beer.cerveza.origin: Mesopotamia and Egypt, c. 4000-3000 BC. The first beers were fermented bread porridges. Sumer had Ninkasi, the goddess dedicated to beer. Egypt paid the pyramid workers in beer. Medieval Europe: monasteries (Belgian Trappists, German Benedictines) perfected brewing. 1516: the Reinheitsgebot (Bavarian Purity Law) rules that beer may contain only water, barley, and hops.
wiki.art.beer.cerveza.production: Malting: barley is soaked, germinated, and kiln-dried (gives color and flavor). Mashing: ground malt + hot water extract sugars (wort). Boiling: hops are added (bitterness, aroma, preservative). Fermentation: yeast turns sugars into alcohol + CO₂. Ale = top fermentation (Saccharomyces cerevisiae, 15-24°C, 5-7 days — fruity, complex). Lager = bottom fermentation (S. pastorianus, 7-13°C, weeks — clean, crisp). Conditioning, filtering, and packaging.
wiki.art.beer.cerveza.tasting: Pilsner: golden, crisp, floral hops, dry, clean finish. IPA: amber-gold, intense hops (citrus, tropical, pine), pronounced bitterness. Wheat: hazy, banana, clove, soft and refreshing. Stout: opaque black, roasted coffee, chocolate, creamy. Porter: dark brown, caramel, nut, soft coffee. Belgian Tripel: strong gold, fruit, spice, honey, effervescent. Sour/Lambic: acidic, complex, funk, fruit. The diversity of styles is infinite — each one is a world.
wiki.art.beer.cerveza.tips: Serve each style at its temperature: lagers 3-5°C, pale ales 7-10°C, stouts 10-13°C, Belgians 8-12°C. The glass matters: pilsner in a tall glass, IPA in a tulip, stout in a pint, wheat in a weizen glass, Belgians in a chalice. Always pour at a 45° tilt, straightening to form two fingers of foam. Guinness: pour in two stages (fill ¾, wait, top up). Michelada: use a light beer (Corona, Modelo Especial). A strong beer list is as important as the cocktail menu.
wiki.art.beer.cerveza.types: LAGERS: Pilsner (Pilsner Urquell, Heineken — golden, hoppy, crisp). Helles (Munich — soft malt, low hops). Vienna Lager (amber, caramel — Negra Modelo). Bock/Doppelbock (strong, malty — Paulaner Salvator). ALES: Pale Ale/IPA (hoppy, citrus, tropical — Sierra Nevada, Punk IPA). Wheat Beer/Weizen (wheat, banana, clove — Paulaner, Hoegaarden). Stout (dark, coffee, chocolate — Guinness). Porter (dark, lighter than stout). Belgian (Dubbel, Tripel, Quad — Chimay, Westmalle). Sour/Lambic (acidic, spontaneous fermentation — Cantillon).
wiki.art.beer.cerveza.cocktails: Michelada (beer, lime, salt, hot sauce, Worcestershire, Clamato — the Mexican Bloody Mary with beer). Shandy (beer + lemonade 1:1 — universal and refreshing). Radler (beer + lemon soda — German tradition). Snakebite (lager + cider 1:1 — British). Black Velvet (stout + champagne — elegant and surprising). Boilermaker (whiskey shot + beer — working-class tradition). Beer Margarita (beer, tequila, lime, lemonade concentrate).
wiki.art.beer.sidra.description: Cider is an alcoholic drink (4-8% ABV) made by fermenting apple juice (and sometimes pear — then called perry/perada). It is the most important fermented beverage after beer and wine, with a thousand-year tradition in Asturias, the Basque Country, Normandy, Brittany, and the British Isles. In bartending, cider is the base of Snakebite, Kir Normand, and many autumn spritzers.
wiki.art.beer.sidra.history: 1st century BC: Celts in northern Hispania and Gaul ferment apples. 1066: the Normans bring the cider tradition to England. 13th century: cider becomes the main drink in Asturias, Normandy, and western England. 1760s: the Bulmer family founds the first commercial cider house in Herefordshire. 20th century: Strongbow and Magners popularize commercial cider. 2010s: the craft cider boom restores diversity — natural, dry, quality ciders.
wiki.art.beer.sidra.origin: Atlantic Europe: Asturias and Basque Country (Spain), Normandy and Brittany (France), England (Somerset, Herefordshire), Ireland. Cider apples are specific varieties — bitter, acidic, and tannic, different from table apples. Asturias has more than 200 native varieties. Normandy distills Calvados from its cider. In England the tradition traces back to the Norman conquest (1066).
wiki.art.beer.sidra.production: Cider apples are washed, crushed, and pressed to obtain the must. Natural fermentation (wild yeasts) or controlled (added yeasts) for weeks or months. Asturian/natural cider: spontaneous fermentation with no additions, no added carbonation. Commercial cider: added carbonation, filtered, pasteurized. Pear cider (perry): same process with specific pears. ABV usually 4-8%. The best ciders are dry, complex, and have no added sugar.
wiki.art.beer.sidra.tasting: Asturian natural cider: acidic apple, yeast, earthy, tannic, dry, subtle natural fizz. Normandy cidre: sweet-tart apple, floral, lightly sparkling, elegant. English dry: crisp apple, tannins, dry and refreshing. Commercial sweet cider: candied apple, pronounced sweetness, carbonated. Perry: fresh pear, floral, light. Ice cider: concentrated apple, honey, raisins — a liquid dessert. The diversity between ciders is as wide as between wines.
wiki.art.beer.sidra.tips: Asturian cider is "escanciada": pour from a height with an extended arm into a wide glass to oxygenate and release aromas — drink immediately in one gulp (culín). Always serve dry cider well chilled (5-7°C). For cocktails, use dry cider (never sweet) — Strongbow Dry or Aspall are solid options. The Snakebite is built by pouring the cider first, then slowly layering the lager on top. An opened natural cider should be consumed the same day. El Gaitero and Trabanco are Asturian benchmarks.
wiki.art.beer.sidra.types: Asturian natural cider (dry, acidic, hazy, still — escanciada). Basque cider (sagardoa — similar to Asturian). Normandy/Breton cidre (slightly sweet, sparkling, low ABV — Pays d'Auge is the premium). English cider (dry or sweet, carbonated — Strongbow, Aspall). Irish cider (Bulmers/Magners — sweeter). Swedish cider (Kopparberg — fruity, sweet). Perry/Perada (pear — Babycham, Oliver's). Ice cider (Canada — frozen apples, sweet and concentrated like an eiswein).
wiki.art.beer.sidra.cocktails: Snakebite (lager + cider 1:1 — British, controversial; some pubs ban it). Kir Normand (crème de cassis + cider — the Norman version of the Kir). Calvados & Cider (Calvados in hot cider — warming in winter). Cider Spritz (dry cider + Aperol + soda — autumn aperitif). Stone Fence (bourbon + cider — a colonial American cocktail). Apple Mojito (rum, mint, lime, cider instead of soda). Wassail (hot cider + spices + roasted apple — English Christmas punch).
wiki.art.wines.sherry.sub: The most versatile fortified wine in the world
wiki.art.wines.sherry.description: Sherry (jerez in Spanish) is a fortified wine with protected designation of origin, produced exclusively in the "sherry triangle" (Jerez de la Frontera, El Puerto de Santa María, and Sanlúcar de Barrameda) in Andalusia. From dry, mineral fino to honey-sweet PX, sherry offers the broadest range of any wine. In modern bartending, fino and manzanilla are the new stars — Sherry Cobbler, Adonis, Bamboo, and Rebujito.
wiki.art.wines.sherry.history: 8th century: the Moors plant vines in Sherish (Jerez). 1587: Sir Francis Drake sacks Cádiz and takes 2,900 barrels — England discovers sherry. 17th-19th centuries: sherry becomes the favorite wine of the English aristocracy (Shakespeare mentions it repeatedly). 1860s: phylloxera destroys the vineyards; they are replanted with Palomino. 20th century: decline due to overproduction and poor quality. 2010s: the sherry renaissance — bartenders and sommeliers rediscover fino and manzanilla as gastronomic and cocktail wines.
wiki.art.wines.sherry.origin: Marco de Jerez, Cádiz, Andalusia, Spain. The triangle between Jerez de la Frontera, El Puerto de Santa María, and Sanlúcar de Barrameda, with albariza (white chalk) soils that retain moisture. The Palomino Fino grape is dominant (95%); Pedro Ximénez and Moscatel are used for sweet wines. The warm climate with the easterly levante wind and the Atlantic westerly (poniente) breeze creates unique conditions for the solera system and biological ageing under flor.
wiki.art.wines.sherry.production: Palomino grapes are pressed and fermented to a dry base wine (11-12% ABV). It is fortified with wine spirit: to 15-15.5% for biological ageing (fino, manzanilla — the flor yeast protects the wine) or to 17%+ for oxidative ageing (oloroso, palo cortado — no flor). Solera and criaderas system: barrels are stacked by age; wine is drawn from the oldest and topped up from the next — ensuring consistency year after year. PX: Pedro Ximénez grapes sun-dried (pasificadas) before pressing.
wiki.art.wines.sherry.tasting: Fino: fresh almond, bread yeast, mineral, saline, dry, clean finish. Manzanilla: lighter than fino, sea breeze, chamomile (the flor), subtle iodine. Amontillado: toasted hazelnut, caramel, spice, complex balance between biological and oxidative. Oloroso: walnut, dried fruit, tobacco, leather, cocoa — powerful and long. PX: raisins, figs, honey, chocolate, molasses — thick as syrup. Palo Cortado: the most complex — elegant nose, powerful palate.
wiki.art.wines.sherry.tips: Fino and manzanilla must be served VERY cold (5-7°C) and consumed within 1-2 days after opening — they are the most fragile wines in the world. Always keep them refrigerated. Amontillado and oloroso last weeks once opened. PX over vanilla ice cream is an instant, spectacular dessert. The Rebujito is perfect for summer events and fiestas. Tio Pepe (fino) and La Guita (manzanilla) are the accessible references. Lustau and Equipo Navazos for exceptional quality.
wiki.art.wines.sherry.types: Fino (15% ABV, under flor, dry, pale, almondy — Tio Pepe, La Ina). Manzanilla (fino from Sanlúcar, saltier and fresher thanks to the sea breeze — La Guita, Papirusa). Amontillado (starts as fino, loses its flor, turns oxidative — dry, hazelnut, amber). Oloroso (oxidative ageing from the start — dark, walnut, dried fruit, dry). Palo Cortado (rare — combines amontillado's nose with oloroso's body). Cream (oloroso + PX, sweet). Pedro Ximénez/PX (ultra-sweet, raisins, honey, chocolate — poured over ice cream).
wiki.art.wines.sherry.cocktails: Sherry Cobbler (amontillado, orange, sugar, berries — the cocktail that popularized the drinking straw in 1840). Adonis (fino, sweet vermouth, orange bitters — low-ABV, elegant). Bamboo (fino, dry vermouth, orange bitters — the low-ABV Martini). Rebujito (fino, 7Up/Sprite, mint, ice — the Andalusian Feria spritz). Sherry Flip (oloroso, egg, sugar, nutmeg). East India (oloroso, sweet vermouth, bitters, maraschino).
wiki.art.wines.port.description: Port wine is a sweet fortified wine produced exclusively in the Douro region of Portugal and aged in the lodges of Vila Nova de Gaia, across the river from the city of Porto. Fermentation is stopped by adding grape spirit, preserving the grape's natural sugar. From young, fruity Ruby to 40+ year-old Vintage Port, it is one of the world's great wines.
wiki.art.wines.port.history: 1386: the Treaty of Windsor binds Portugal and England commercially. 1678: English merchants discover Douro wine — they add brandy so it survives the sea journey. 1756: the Marquis of Pombal creates the world's first appellation of origin for the Douro. 1800s: the great English houses (Graham's, Taylor's, Dow's, Cockburn's) dominate the trade. 1994: the Douro is declared a UNESCO World Heritage Site. Today: port's rebirth as a cocktail and pairing ingredient.
wiki.art.wines.port.origin: Douro Valley, northern Portugal — one of the oldest and most spectacular vineyards in the world (UNESCO Heritage). Grapes grow on terraces carved into the schist slopes of the Douro. More than 80 native varieties are permitted, with Touriga Nacional, Touriga Franca, Tinta Roriz, Tinto Cão, and Tinta Barroca being the main ones. The ageing cellars are in Vila Nova de Gaia, across the Douro from Porto.
wiki.art.wines.port.production: Hand harvest in September on the Douro terraces. Fermentation is stopped ("mutage") by adding grape spirit (77% ABV) when the must has fermented to 6-9% — the residual sugar is preserved. The resulting wine is 19-22% ABV and naturally sweet. Ruby ports age in large vats (little oxidation, preserving fruit). Tawny ports age in 550L barrels (slow oxidation, developing dried fruit and caramel notes).
wiki.art.wines.port.tasting: Ruby: intense dark fruit (cherry, blackberry, plum), chocolate, spice, juicy tannins. LBV: like ruby but more concentrated and structured. Vintage: extraordinarily complex — dark fruit, violets, chocolate, minerals, silky tannins, decades of evolution. Tawny 10-year: walnut, caramel, candied orange, toffee, dried fruit. Tawny 20+: sublime complexity — honey, hazelnut, noble rancio, Eastern spices. White: citrus, almond, honey.
wiki.art.wines.port.tips: Port & Tonic with white port is the Portuguese aperitif of the moment — serve in a large wine glass with plenty of ice, mint, and orange slice. 10-year tawny is the best introduction to port — perfect balance between fruit and cask. Ruby is too young to sip neat; better in cocktails or with chocolate. A Vintage Port is decanted 2-4 hours before serving. Open tawny keeps for weeks refrigerated. Taylor's, Graham's, Niepoort, and Quinta do Noval are benchmarks.
wiki.art.wines.port.types: Ruby (young, fruity, intense — "Reserva" is the superior selection). Late Bottled Vintage/LBV (4-6 years in vat, more structure). Vintage/Vintage Port (from a single exceptional year, ages 20-40+ years in bottle — the great cellar wine). Tawny (aged in cask — 10, 20, 30, 40-year indications, with walnut and caramel notes). Colheita (single-vintage tawny). White Port (white grapes, dry or sweet — for Port & Tonic). Rosé Port (recent, for spritzers).
wiki.art.wines.port.cocktails: Porto Flip (tawny port, cognac, whole egg, nutmeg — a 19th-century classic, liquid dessert). Port & Tonic (white port, tonic, mint, orange — the trendy aperitif in Portugal). Porto Cobbler (ruby port, orange, sugar, berries). Chicago Fizz (port, rum, lemon, egg white, soda). Bishop (port, orange, spices, hot — winter punch). Port Negus (hot port, sugar, lemon, nutmeg — the classic British hot drink).
wiki.art.wines.madeira.sub: The indestructible wine from the Atlantic island
wiki.art.wines.madeira.description: Madeira is a fortified wine produced on the Portuguese island of Madeira, in the Atlantic. It is the most resilient wine in the world — 100+ year-old bottles are still drinkable thanks to its unique heating process (estufagem). From dry Sercial to sweet Malmsey, it was the favorite wine of the American Founding Fathers.
wiki.art.wines.madeira.history: 1419: the Portuguese plant vines on Madeira. 16th-18th centuries: the heat in ship holds improves the wine — they discover estufagem. 1776: the Founding Fathers toasted with Madeira when signing the Declaration of Independence. 1800s: phylloxera and oidium devastate the vineyards. 21st century: revival as a cult wine.
wiki.art.wines.madeira.origin: Madeira Island, Portugal (Atlantic archipelago, 600 km west of Morocco). Discovered in 1419. Terraced vineyards (poios). The four noble varieties: Sercial (dry), Verdelho (off-dry), Bual (semi-sweet), Malmsey/Malvasia (sweet). Tinta Negra is the most planted grape (85%).
wiki.art.wines.madeira.production: Fermentation is partially stopped with grape spirit. Estufagem: the wine is heated to 45-50°C for 3+ months. Canteiro: the premium method, ageing under the roof with natural heating. The heat caramelizes sugars and oxidizes the wine in a controlled way — making it practically indestructible. An opened bottle lasts years.
wiki.art.wines.madeira.tasting: Sercial: citrus, green walnut, almond, vibrant acidity, dry. Verdelho: orange, caramel, smoke. Bual: toffee, chocolate, dried fruit. Malmsey: figs, raisins, molasses, dark chocolate, dense. All share high acidity, toasted notes from estufagem, and extraordinary longevity.
wiki.art.wines.madeira.tips: An open bottle lasts months or years without degrading — perfect for bars with low turnover. Chilled Sercial as an aperitif; Malmsey at room temperature as a digestif. Frasqueiras from the early 1900s are among the oldest drinkable wines in the world. Blandy's and Henriques & Henriques are the references. Madeira Punch is a historical talking point — Washington and Jefferson drank it.
wiki.art.wines.madeira.types: Sercial (dry, acidic, almondy — aperitif). Verdelho (off-dry, citrus, honey). Bual (semi-sweet, caramel, chocolate). Malmsey (sweet, molasses, figs — dessert). Rainwater (light, off-dry). Colheita (single vintage, 5+ years). Frasqueira/Vintage (single vintage, 20+ years — bottles of 50-100+ years are possible).
wiki.art.wines.madeira.cocktails: Madeira Punch (Madeira, lemon, sugar, spices, hot water — George Washington's punch). Baltimore Eggnog (Madeira, cognac, rum, eggs, milk). Prince of Wales (Madeira, champagne, curaçao, Angostura). Madeira is more gastronomic than cocktail-focused, but its place in historical punches is essential.
wiki.art.wines.lillet.description: Lillet is a French aperitif made from Bordeaux wine flavored with fruit liqueurs and citrus peels. Maison Lillet was founded in 1872, but the Kina Lillet aperitif itself — lighter and fruitier than vermouth — didn't arrive until 1887. Its elegant profile made it James Bond's secret ingredient (Vesper Martini); its delicacy makes it perfect on the rocks or in sophisticated cocktails.
wiki.art.wines.lillet.history: 1872: brothers Paul and Raymond Lillet found Maison Lillet in Podensac as a wine and liqueur business. 1887: they create Kina Lillet, the Bordeaux-based aperitif with quinine. 1895: it is exported to the French colonies as a tonic against malaria. 1953: Ian Fleming specifies "Kina Lillet" in the Vesper Martini recipe in Casino Royale. 1986: reformulated — less quinine, fruitier — and renamed simply "Lillet". 2011: Lillet Rosé becomes an instant hit. Today it is an essential ingredient in the White Negroni.
wiki.art.wines.lillet.origin: Podensac, Bordeaux, France. Brothers Paul and Raymond Lillet founded the house in 1872, but the Kina Lillet aperitif — a blend of Bordeaux wines, sweet and bitter orange liqueurs, and quinine — didn't arrive until 1887. The original formula contained more quinine; today's version (reformulated in 1986) is softer and fruitier.
wiki.art.wines.lillet.production: Base of Sémillon and Sauvignon white wines from Bordeaux (85%). Sweet oranges from Spain, bitter oranges from Haiti, and Peruvian quinine are separately macerated in grape spirit. The wine is then blended with the macerated fruit liqueurs. Ageing in oak tanks for months. Bottled at 17% ABV. Each expression (Blanc, Rosé, Rouge) uses a different wine base.
wiki.art.wines.lillet.tasting: Blanc: nose of orange-blossom honey, sweet citrus, white peach. On the palate: smooth, fruity entry, light bitterness from orange peel, clean refreshing finish. Rosé: fresh strawberry, pink grapefruit, spring flowers, lively finish. Rouge: ripe red fruit (cherry, currant), soft spice, silky tannins, a longer more complex finish. All three share a characteristic Bordeaux elegance.
wiki.art.wines.lillet.tips: Always serve very cold (6-8°C) — straight from the fridge. Lillet Blanc on the rocks with an orange or cucumber slice is the simplest, most elegant aperitif. Refrigerate after opening; consume within 3-4 weeks. It is not interchangeable with dry vermouth — Lillet is sweeter and fruitier. In the Vesper, the original recipe calls for "Kina Lillet" which no longer exists; Lillet Blanc + a dash of quinine bitters comes closer. Some bartenders use Lillet Rouge in Negronis for a Bordeaux twist.
wiki.art.wines.lillet.types: Lillet Blanc (the original — white wine, citrus, honey, floral, the most versatile in bartending). Lillet Rosé (2011 — strawberry, raspberry, pink grapefruit, perfect for summer). Lillet Rouge (red wine, red fruit, spice, more complex and less known). All three serve at 6-8°C. Lillet Blanc is the most used in cocktails (Vesper, White Negroni, Corpse Reviver).
wiki.art.wines.lillet.cocktails: Vesper Martini (gin, vodka, Lillet Blanc — "shaken, not stirred," James Bond). Corpse Reviver No. 2 (gin, Lillet Blanc, Cointreau, lemon, absinthe — a revived classic). White Negroni (gin, Suze, Lillet Blanc — the modern reinvention). Lillet Spritz (Lillet, tonic or soda, orange slice — the perfect French aperitif). Lillet Vive (Lillet Blanc, tonic, cucumber, strawberry, mint — the brand's official serve).
wiki.art.wines.dubonnet.description: Dubonnet is a French wine-based aperitif flavored with quinine, herbs, and spices. Created as a malaria tonic for French colonial troops, it became the favorite aperitif of Queen Elizabeth II of England (always paired with gin). It is sweeter and spicier than vermouth, with a subtle quinine bitterness that makes it unique among aperitif wines.
wiki.art.wines.dubonnet.history: 1846: Joseph Dubonnet creates the quinine-laced aperitif for the colonial troops in Algeria. 1860s: it becomes popular in Parisian cafés as an elegant aperitif. 1900s: it is exported to London and becomes a favorite of British high society. 1940s-2022: Queen Elizabeth II drinks her daily "Dubonnet & Gin" before lunch — a royal ritual spanning decades. 2000s: the cocktail revival movement rediscovers Dubonnet as an ingredient in classic cocktails.
wiki.art.wines.dubonnet.origin: Paris, France. Parisian chemist Joseph Dubonnet created the formula in 1846, commissioned by the French government, which was looking for a way to make quinine palatable for soldiers in North Africa. Quinine prevented malaria but was extremely bitter — Dubonnet masked it with sweet wine, herbs, and spices.
wiki.art.wines.dubonnet.production: Base of red wine (Dubonnet Rouge) or white wine (Dubonnet Blanc) from the Languedoc-Roussillon region. Quinine (cinchona bark), green coffee, cacao, cinnamon, chamomile, and other herbs are added. Extended maceration in fortified wine. Lightly sweetened and bottled at 14.8% ABV. The American version (made under license) has a slightly different profile from the original French.
wiki.art.wines.dubonnet.tasting: Rouge: aroma of ripe red fruit, chocolate, coffee, warm spices (cinnamon, clove). On the palate: balanced sweet-bitter, candied cherry, subtle quinine, Mediterranean herbs, spicy lingering finish. Blanc: lighter, white flowers, citrus, honey, delicate bitterness. The profile is richer and sweeter than red vermouth, with extra complexity from the quinine and cacao.
wiki.art.wines.dubonnet.tips: Serve cold (6-8°C), on the rocks with a slice of lemon. The classic Dubonnet & Gin ratio is 1:1, but Queen Elizabeth took it 2:1 (more Dubonnet). Refrigerate after opening; lasts 2-3 weeks. Dubonnet can replace sweet vermouth in any cocktail for a spicier, quinine-forward profile. The French version is superior to the American — look for the import. Cocchi Americano is the closest alternative if Dubonnet is unavailable.
wiki.art.wines.dubonnet.types: Dubonnet Rouge (the original — red wine, quinine, spices, sweet-bitter, deep ruby color). Dubonnet Blanc (white version — lighter, floral, less known). Dubonnet Gold (limited edition, aged). Belongs to the "quinquinas" family of quinine-laced wines, along with Lillet (Kina Lillet), Bonal, Cocchi Americano, and Byrrh. Dubonnet Rouge is the standard for the classic recipe.
wiki.art.wines.dubonnet.cocktails: Dubonnet & Gin (Dubonnet Rouge, gin 1:1, lemon slice — Queen Elizabeth II's cocktail). Dubonnet Manhattan (Dubonnet replaces sweet vermouth — more complex). Zaza Cocktail (Dubonnet, gin, orange bitters — pre-Prohibition classic). Opera Cocktail (gin, Dubonnet, maraschino — elegant and forgotten). BLT Cocktail (bourbon, Lillet, tonic, Dubonnet float). Napoleon Cocktail (gin, Dubonnet, Fernet — potent).
wiki.art.amaros.amaro-italiano.descripti: Italian amaro is a broad category of bitter herbal liqueurs, traditionally consumed as a digestif after meals. Every Italian region has its own distinctive amaros, from sweet Sicilian Averna to elegant Friulian Nonino. They are the soul of Italy's after-dinner ritual.
wiki.art.amaros.amaro-italiano.history: 13th century: Italian monks craft medicinal herbal elixirs. 1815: Gaspare Campari creates his bitter (see separate article). 1868: Salvatore Averna receives the recipe from Benedictine monks in Sicily. 1885: Stanislao Cobianchi creates Amaro Montenegro in Bologna. 1897: Ausano Ramazzotti launches his amaro in Milan. 1973: the Nonino family creates the first amaro based on single-varietal grappa. 2010s: amaros take over craft bartending worldwide.
wiki.art.amaros.amaro-italiano.origin: All of Italy. Amaros were born as herbal medicines in medieval monasteries and pharmacies. Every region developed its own style: Sicily (Averna), Bologna (Montenegro), Friuli (Nonino), Milan (Ramazzotti), Calabria (Vecchio Amaro del Capo), Lombardy (Braulio), Basilicata (Lucano).
wiki.art.amaros.amaro-italiano.productio: Base of neutral alcohol or wine in which herbs, roots, barks, flowers, and spices (gentian, rhubarb, quinine, angelica, thistle, mint, citrus) are macerated. Filtered, sweetened with syrup or caramel, and briefly aged. Each amaro has its secret recipe. Typical ABV: 16-40%.
wiki.art.amaros.amaro-italiano.tasting: Averna: candied orange, caramel, sweet herbs, smooth finish. Montenegro: perfect sweet-bitter balance, orange, vanilla, rose, spice. Nonino: elegant grappa, alpine herbs, honey, long refined finish. Ramazzotti: bitter orange, gentian, licorice. Braulio: mint, gentian, alpine pine, intense bitterness. Each one is its own universe.
wiki.art.amaros.amaro-italiano.tips: Montenegro is the most versatile amaro in cocktails: it works as a sweet-vermouth substitute in almost anything. Nonino is the premium sipper. Averna is perfect for amaro newcomers (sweeter). Serve at room temperature or with a large ice cube. Exploring regional amaros is exploring the geography of Italy.
wiki.art.amaros.amaro-italiano.types: Averna (Sicily, sweet, orange, herbs, 29% ABV). Montenegro (Bologna, balanced, 40 botanicals, 23% ABV — "the perfect amaro"). Nonino Quintessentia (Friuli, grappa base, elegant, 35% ABV). Ramazzotti (Milan, bitter orange, 30% ABV). Braulio (Alpine Valtellina, mountain herbs, 21% ABV). Lucano (Basilicata, minty). Vecchio Amaro del Capo (Calabria, fresh herbal).
wiki.art.amaros.amaro-italiano.cocktails: Paper Plane (bourbon, Amaro Nonino, Aperol, lemon — equal parts, the cocktail that put Nonino on the map). Black Manhattan (rye, Averna, Angostura — Amaro replacing sweet vermouth). Montenegro Sour (Montenegro, lemon, syrup, egg white). Bicicletta (Campari or amaro, white wine, soda — rural Italian aperitif). Amaro on the rocks with an orange peel — the classic Italian after-dinner sip.
wiki.art.amaros.amaro-nonino.sub: The Friulian amaro of the Paper Plane
wiki.art.amaros.amaro-nonino.description: Amaro Nonino Quintessentia is a premium Italian amaro (35% ABV) from Friuli-Venezia Giulia, made on an aged grappa base and infused with alpine herbs, roots, and barks. It is the amaro that conquered modern bartending thanks to the Paper Plane — Sam Ross's cocktail that became an instant modern classic. Its profile is more elegant and fruity than other Italian amari, with exceptional balance.
wiki.art.amaros.amaro-nonino.history: 1897: Orazio Nonino founds the distillery in Percoto. 1973: Giannola Nonino creates the first single-varietal grappa (Picolit) — a revolution in the grappa world. 1990s: she creates Amaro Nonino Quintessentia on an aged grappa base. 2007: Sam Ross creates the Paper Plane (bourbon, Nonino, Aperol, lemon) at Milk & Honey in NYC — the cocktail that made Nonino globally famous. 2010s-present: it becomes the most in-demand amaro for bartenders worldwide.
wiki.art.amaros.amaro-nonino.origin: Percoto, Friuli-Venezia Giulia, northeastern Italy. The Nonino family is one of the most respected dynasties in Italian distillation — famous for their single-varietal grappas that revolutionized the industry. Giannola Nonino created Amaro Quintessentia in the 1990s, using native-variety grappa as a base instead of the usual neutral alcohol, giving the amaro unique depth and elegance.
wiki.art.amaros.amaro-nonino.production: Base of aged grape grappa (not neutral alcohol like most amari). Infused with alpine herbs from Friuli, roots (gentian, rhubarb), citrus peels, and spices. Rested in oak barrels to soften and integrate. Bottled at 35% ABV. The grappa base is what sets Nonino apart from every other amaro — it adds a vinous fruit depth that neutral alcohol cannot deliver.
wiki.art.amaros.amaro-nonino.tasting: Aroma: candied orange, caramel, alpine herbs, honey, a touch of grappa. Palate: sweet-fruity entry (orange, caramel), evolves into elegant bitter herbs (gentian, rhubarb), warm spices, a vinous grappa base. Finish: long, balanced bitter-sweet, with lasting orange and herbs. It is notably more elegant and less aggressively bitter than Fernet or Campari — the sophisticated bartender's amaro.
wiki.art.amaros.amaro-nonino.tips: The Paper Plane is a must on any serious bar menu — equal parts of everything, shaken, strained, served up. Nonino is the amaro that converts skeptics — its fruity elegance is approachable without losing complexity. Do not substitute another amaro in the Paper Plane — Montenegro is similar but not the same. Store at room temperature. More expensive than other amari, but justified by the grappa base. It is professional bartenders' favorite amaro for a reason.
wiki.art.amaros.amaro-nonino.types: Amaro Nonino Quintessentia (35% ABV — the flagship product and the only one that matters in cocktails). The Nonino family also makes: Grappa Nonino (single-varietal from Moscato, Prosecco, Picolit — among the best in Italy). ÙE (honey-and-herb liqueur). Gioiello (light amaro). But Quintessentia is the star and the one every bartender needs.
wiki.art.amaros.amaro-nonino.cocktails: Paper Plane (bourbon, Amaro Nonino, Aperol, lemon — equal parts, the quintessential modern classic, created by Sam Ross). Naked & Famous (mezcal, Nonino, yellow Chartreuse, lime — the mezcal version of the Paper Plane). Black Manhattan (rye, Nonino replaces sweet vermouth, bitters — more bitter and complex). Nonino Spritz (Nonino, prosecco, soda — Friulian aperitif). Nonino Old Fashioned (Nonino as the base, sugar, bitters).
wiki.art.amaros.angostura-bitters.descri: Angostura Aromatic Bitters are the most important and iconic bitters in the cocktail world. Their oversized label (a famous design error that stuck) and secret herb-and-spice content make them unmistakable. They are essential in the Old Fashioned, Manhattan, Whiskey Sour, and dozens of classic cocktails.
wiki.art.amaros.angostura-bitters.histor: 1824: Dr. Siegert creates the bitters in Angostura, Venezuela, as a tonic for Bolívar's troops. 1830: commercial sales begin. 1875: the Siegert family emigrates to Trinidad after Venezuelan political turmoil. 1900: the oversized label (a design-contest mistake) is kept as brand identity. 20th century: they become the global standard for aromatic bitters.
wiki.art.amaros.angostura-bitters.origin: Ciudad Bolívar (formerly Angostura), Venezuela. Dr. Johann Gottlieb Benjamin Siegert, a German military surgeon in Simón Bolívar's army, created the formula in 1824 as a medicinal tonic. Production moved to Trinidad and Tobago in 1875 and continues there to this day.
wiki.art.amaros.angostura-bitters.produc: The exact recipe is secret, known only to 5 people. It is known to include gentian, cinnamon, clove, cardamom, bitter orange peel, and other herbs and spices, macerated in high-proof alcohol (44.7% ABV). Despite the high ABV, it is used in dashes, not sipped neat.
wiki.art.amaros.angostura-bitters.tastin: Aromatic: intense warm spice (cinnamon, clove, cardamom), bitter gentian, herbs, orange peel, long spicy finish. Orange: concentrated bitter orange, cardamom, soft spices. Cocoa: bitter cacao, vanilla, warm spices. All three are ultra-concentrated — a dash transforms a cocktail.
wiki.art.amaros.angostura-bitters.tips: 2-3 dashes are enough in most cocktails — bitters are concentrated. A dash ≈ 1ml. No Angostura, no Old Fashioned and no Manhattan. Orange Bitters are perfect in dry Martinis. Store at room temperature; they keep indefinitely. The Trinidad Sour (1oz Angostura as the base) is the ultimate test for bitter lovers.
wiki.art.amaros.angostura-bitters.types: Angostura Aromatic Bitters (the original, oversized white label, 44.7% ABV), Angostura Orange Bitters (orange, launched in 2007, 28% ABV), Angostura Cocoa Bitters (cacao, launched in 2019). All three are essentials in a professional bar. There are hundreds of bitters brands, but Angostura is king.
wiki.art.amaros.angostura-bitters.cockta: Old Fashioned (whiskey, sugar, 2-3 dashes Angostura — the oldest cocktail). Manhattan (rye, sweet vermouth, 2 dashes Angostura). Whiskey Sour (with Angostura on the foam as a decoration). Pink Gin (gin, Angostura — a Royal Navy classic). Champagne Cocktail (champagne, sugar, Angostura). Trinidad Sour (30ml of Angostura bitters as the base — the most extreme cocktail).
wiki.art.amaros.aperol.description: Aperol is a bright-orange Italian bitter liqueur, softer and sweeter than Campari (11% ABV). Created in 1919 in Padua, it became a global phenomenon thanks to the Aperol Spritz, the most popular cocktail of the 2010s.
wiki.art.amaros.aperol.history: 1919: the Barbieri brothers launch Aperol at the Padua Fair. 1950s: Aperol becomes a popular aperitif in northeastern Italy. 2003: Campari Group acquires the brand. 2000s-2010s: the Aperol Spritz conquers Europe and then the world, becoming synonymous with the summer aperitif. 2019: Aperol's centenary; global sales have multiplied by 10 in a decade.
wiki.art.amaros.aperol.origin: Padua, Veneto, Italy. Created by brothers Luigi and Silvio Barbieri in 1919 and presented at the Padua Fair. The orange color comes from an infusion of bitter oranges, gentian, rhubarb, and herbs. Today owned by Campari Group.
wiki.art.amaros.aperol.production: Infusion of bitter and sweet oranges, gentian, rhubarb, quinine, and a secret herb blend in alcohol. The exact recipe is secret. Lower in ABV (11%) and less bitter than Campari, which makes it more approachable for the mainstream drinker.
wiki.art.amaros.aperol.tasting: Bitter orange, grapefruit, soft herbs, gentian, rhubarb, moderate sweetness, a light and approachable bitterness. Vibrant orange color. Short, refreshing finish. Far less bitter than Campari — the "gateway" to the world of bitter liqueurs.
wiki.art.amaros.aperol.tips: Perfect Spritz: large wine glass with lots of ice, 90ml prosecco, 60ml Aperol, splash of soda, orange slice. Order matters: ice, prosecco, Aperol, soda. Do not shake. Select is the authentic Venetian alternative for a more bitter, complex Spritz. Aperol fades in the light: store in a dark place.
wiki.art.amaros.aperol.types: Aperol (the single product, 11% ABV). No official variants. Aperol Spritz pre-mixed (ready to drink, in bottle and can). Segment competitors: Select (another Venetian aperitif, more complex), Cappelletti (Trentino aperitif).
wiki.art.amaros.aperol.cocktails: Aperol Spritz (Aperol, prosecco, soda — 3:2:1, in a wine glass with ice and an orange slice — THE cocktail of summer). Naked & Famous (mezcal, yellow Chartreuse, Aperol, lime). Paper Plane (bourbon, Aperol, Amaro Nonino, lemon — equal parts). Division Bell (mezcal, Aperol, maraschino, lime).
wiki.art.amaros.becherovka.sub: The Czech herbal liqueur from Karlovy Vary
wiki.art.amaros.becherovka.description: Becherovka is a Czech herbal liqueur (38% ABV) produced exclusively in Karlovy Vary (Carlsbad) since 1807. With a profile dominated by cinnamon, clove, and more than 20 herbs, it is the Czech national digestif and the most famous Central European amaro. The Beton (Becherovka + tonic) is the quintessential Czech highball — refreshing, herbal, and surprisingly versatile.
wiki.art.amaros.becherovka.history: 1807: Josef Becher creates "English Bitter" in his Karlovy Vary pharmacy. 1841: His son Johann Becher industrializes production. 1890s: it becomes the standard digestif of the Austro-Hungarian Empire. 1945: nationalized by the communist government. 1997: privatized; acquired by Pernod Ricard in 2001. Today: sold in 35+ countries. The Beton (Becherovka + tonic) became popular in the 2000s as an alternative to the G&T.
wiki.art.amaros.becherovka.origin: Karlovy Vary (Carlsbad), Bohemia, Czech Republic. Josef Vitus Becher, a pharmacist, created the recipe in 1807 with the help of English doctor Christian Frobrig, who visited the thermal spas of Karlovy Vary. The formula uses the local thermal waters as an ingredient. The original distillery is still in Karlovy Vary and can be visited.
wiki.art.amaros.becherovka.production: More than 20 herbs and spices (the full recipe is known by only 2 people): dominant Ceylon cinnamon, clove, anise, cardamom, allspice, ginger, and aromatic herbs. They are macerated in alcohol and thermal water from Karlovy Vary. Blended with sugar. Rested in Slovak oak barrels for 2 months. Bottled at 38% ABV. The local thermal water is considered an essential part of the recipe.
wiki.art.amaros.becherovka.tasting: Aroma: intense cinnamon, clove, Christmas spices, herbs, a balsamic medicinal touch. Palate: dominant cinnamon and clove, balanced sweetness, underlying bitter herbs, warm spices. Finish: long, warm, lingering cinnamon over an herbal base. It is like liquid Christmas — spiced, warm, and comforting. Sweeter than Jägermeister, spicier than Fernet.
wiki.art.amaros.becherovka.tips: The Beton (Becherovka + tonic 1:3) is mandatory for any bartender — refreshing and unique. Serve the Original cold (from the freezer) as a digestif after dinner. Becherovka with hot apple cider is the perfect winter grog. The tour of the Becherovka museum in Karlovy Vary includes a tasting. Keep in the freezer for shots. It naturally pairs with apple, cinnamon, honey, and citrus. It is the most popular souvenir in the Czech Republic.
wiki.art.amaros.becherovka.types: Becherovka Original (38% ABV — the classic, dominant cinnamon). Becherovka Lemond (20% ABV — with lemon, lighter, for summer). Becherovka KV 14 (14% ABV — a soft version, aperitif). Becherovka Ice & Fire (30% ABV — with menthol, for cold shots). The Original is the only one that matters for serious bartending. The variants are more for casual drinking.
wiki.art.amaros.becherovka.cocktails: Beton (Becherovka + tonic + lemon slice — "concrete" in Czech, the national highball). Becherovka Mule (Becherovka, ginger beer, lime — a spiced Moscow Mule). Becherovka Old Fashioned (Becherovka, bourbon, bitters — warm and spiced). Hot Becherovka (Becherovka, hot water, honey, lemon — perfect in winter). Czech Christmas (Becherovka, apple, cinnamon, champagne). Becherovka Sour (Becherovka, lemon, syrup, egg white).
wiki.art.amaros.campari.sub: The iconic red bitter from Milan
wiki.art.amaros.campari.description: Until 2006, Campari's red came from cochineal — a beetle. Today it's artificial colour, but the character is unchanged: dry-bitter, spiced, with a sweetness that stops just shy of cloying. It's the best-selling aperitif in the world and the backbone of the Negroni, Americano, and Spritz. If the first sip stings, take three more — it turns into addiction.
wiki.art.amaros.campari.history: 1860: Gaspare Campari creates the "Bitter all'Uso d'Olanda" in Novara. 1867: he opens Caffè Campari in Milan's Galleria. 1904: Davide Campari (his son) founds the company and begins exporting. 1919: at Caffè Casoni in Florence, Count Camillo Negroni asks Fosco Scarselli for a stronger Americano — Scarselli swaps the soda for gin and the Negroni is born. 1932: the Americano (Campari, vermouth, soda) consolidates as an international apéritif. 2000s: the Aperol Spritz and the Negroni revival send global sales soaring.
wiki.art.amaros.campari.origin: Milan, Italy. Gaspare Campari created the recipe in Novara in 1860 and perfected it at his Caffè Campari in the Galleria Vittorio Emanuele II in Milan, which became the epicenter of Milanese aperitif culture.
wiki.art.amaros.campari.production: The recipe contains more than 60 ingredients — herbs, spices, barks, and fruits — macerated and infused in alcohol. The exact list is secret and known only to the master blender. The original red color came from cochineal carmine; today an artificial colorant is used. 25% ABV.
wiki.art.amaros.campari.tasting: Intense, defined bitterness, bitter orange, chinotto peel, medicinal herbs, licorice, tart cherry. Sweetness that balances the bitterness without dominating it. Bright red color. Long, bitter, dry finish with an aftertaste of bitter citrus and herbs.
wiki.art.amaros.campari.tips: Classic Negroni: 30 ml of each (gin, Campari, sweet vermouth), big block of ice, orange peel expressed over the glass before serving. Garibaldi: whip the orange juice separately until it foams — that "fluffy" texture is what separates a Garibaldi from a screwdriver. Store the bottle at room temperature; cold dulls the bitterness.
wiki.art.amaros.campari.types: Campari (the flagship product, 25% ABV), Campari Soda (pre-mixed in its iconic conical 10cl bottle, designed by Fortunato Depero in 1932), Campari Cask Tales (barrel-aged, limited edition). There are no variants — Campari is Campari. The flavor varies slightly across markets.
wiki.art.amaros.campari.cocktails: Negroni (gin, Campari, sweet vermouth — equal parts, the king of bitterness). Americano (Campari, sweet vermouth, soda — the forerunner of the Negroni). Boulevardier (bourbon, Campari, sweet vermouth — Negroni with whiskey). Campari Spritz (Campari, prosecco, soda). Jungle Bird (dark rum, Campari, pineapple, lime — bitter tiki). Garibaldi (Campari, fresh orange juice — "fluffy orange juice").
wiki.art.amaros.cynar.description: Cynar is an Italian amaro made with artichoke (carciofo) and 12 more herbs and plants. Despite its main ingredient, it does not taste of artichoke: it is herbal, bitter-sweet, and earthy. A bartender favorite for its versatility and complexity.
wiki.art.amaros.cynar.history: 1952: Angelo Dalle Molle creates Cynar in Padua. 1960s-70s: advertising campaigns starring actor Ernesto Calindri drinking Cynar in the middle of traffic make the brand iconic in Italy. 1995: Campari Group acquires the brand. 2010s: bartenders rediscover Cynar as a cocktail ingredient — the Trident and other drinks bring it back into fashion.
wiki.art.amaros.cynar.origin: Padua, Italy. Created by Venetian entrepreneur Angelo Dalle Molle in 1952. The name comes from "Cynara scolymus", the botanical name for artichoke. The artichoke logo on the bottle is unmistakable. Today owned by Campari Group.
wiki.art.amaros.cynar.production: Artichoke (Cynara scolymus) and 12 herbs and plants are macerated in alcohol. The blend is filtered and sweetened. The artichoke gives a unique vegetal-earthy character but not a literal artichoke flavor. 16.5% ABV (standard) or 35% ABV (Cynar 70 Proof).
wiki.art.amaros.cynar.tasting: Herbal, earthy, dark caramel, gentian, subtle vegetal notes (not artichoke-tasting), a moderate and elegant bitterness, hints of dark chocolate. The 70 Proof: everything amplified, drier, more bitter, more complex. Medium-long finish with a herbal aftertaste.
wiki.art.amaros.cynar.tips: Cynar 70 Proof is the version to use in cocktails: more body and bitterness, stands up better to dilution. On the rocks with an orange slice it makes an excellent aperitif. Swap it for Campari in Negronis for a more herbal, less bitter version. Pairs especially well with agave (tequila, mezcal).
wiki.art.amaros.cynar.types: Cynar Original (16.5% ABV, sweeter and lighter), Cynar 70 Proof (35% ABV, more bitter and intense, preferred by bartenders). No other variants. The 70 Proof is significantly better for cocktails.
wiki.art.amaros.cynar.cocktails: Cynar Spritz (Cynar, prosecco, soda — a more bitter alternative to the Aperol Spritz). Trident (aquavit, Cynar, dry sherry, peach bitters — the cocktail that revived Cynar). Rabo de Galo (cachaça, Cynar — the Brazilian Negroni). Cynar Julep (Cynar, bourbon, mint). Cynar on the rocks with orange as an aperitif.
wiki.art.amaros.fernet.sub: The world's most intense digestive bitter
wiki.art.amaros.fernet.description: Fernet-Branca is an Italian amaro of intense bitterness, nearly black color, and a mentholated-herbal profile that makes it unmistakable. It is the most popular digestif in Argentina (where it's consumed more than in Italy) and a cult ingredient in bartending worldwide.
wiki.art.amaros.fernet.history: 1845: Bernardino Branca creates Fernet-Branca in Milan as a "medicinal remedy". 1862: it is presented at the Great Exhibition in London. 1900s: it is exported to Argentina with Italian immigrants. 1980s: Fernet con Coca becomes a cultural phenomenon in Argentina, especially in Córdoba. 2000s: American bartenders adopt Fernet as the industry "handshake" — ordering Fernet shows you know bars.
wiki.art.amaros.fernet.origin: Milan, Italy. Created by Bernardino Branca in 1845. The Branca family has kept the secret recipe ever since. Argentina is the world's largest consumer of Fernet-Branca, where it is mixed with Coca-Cola as the unofficial national drink.
wiki.art.amaros.fernet.production: 27 herbs and spices from 4 continents, including myrrh, rhubarb, chamomile, cardamom, aloe, saffron, and mint. They are macerated in grape alcohol, distilled, and aged in oak barrels for at least a year. 39% ABV. The exact recipe is known only by the president of Branca and the master distiller.
wiki.art.amaros.fernet.tasting: Intense mint, eucalyptus, myrrh, medicinal herbs, licorice, extreme bitterness, notes of camphor and mushroom. Dense, almost viscous texture. Ultra-long finish, mentholated and bitter, with a "medicinal" effect that divides opinion. An acquired taste — you either love it or hate it.
wiki.art.amaros.fernet.tips: Argentine Fernet con Coca: 30% Fernet, 70% Coke, lots of ice, in a tall glass. The Hanky Panky only needs 2 bar spoons of Fernet — it is very potent. As a neat digestif, a cold shot after a heavy meal is unbeatable. If the bitterness is too much, start with Branca Menta.
wiki.art.amaros.fernet.types: Fernet-Branca (the original, 39% ABV, ultra-bitter), Branca Menta (with mint, sweeter and more approachable, 28% ABV), Argentine Fernet-Branca (slightly different formulation, locally produced). Other fernets: Fernet Stock (Czech), Fernet 1882 (Argentine), Luxardo Fernet. Branca is the benchmark.
wiki.art.amaros.fernet.cocktails: Fernet con Coca (Fernet-Branca, Coca-Cola, ice — the Argentine national cocktail). Hanky Panky (gin, sweet vermouth, two dashes of Fernet — created by Ada Coleman at the Savoy in 1903). Toronto (Canadian whisky, Fernet, sugar, Angostura). Industry Sour (Fernet, green Chartreuse, lime, syrup). As a shot: the bartenders' "handshake".
wiki.map.advocaat.desc: Dutch liqueur made from egg yolks, sugar, and brandy. Custard-like texture.
wiki.map.airag.desc: Fermented mare's milk of the Mongolian nomads. 2-3% alcohol, national drink for millennia.
wiki.map.alentejo.desc: Warm plains of southern Portugal. Ripe reds and traditional vinification in talha clay amphorae.
wiki.map.allspice-dram.desc: Jamaican liqueur of allspice berries and rum. Tiki cocktail staple (Pimento Dram).
wiki.map.alsace.desc: Aromatic Riesling, Gewürztraminer, and Pinot Gris on the Franco-German border.
wiki.map.amarula.desc: South African cream with marula fruit. Elephants also enjoy it wild.
wiki.map.ancho-reyes.desc: Artisanal Mexican liqueur of ancho chili. 1927 Puebla recipe revived in 2013.
wiki.map.applejack.desc: American apple brandy (jack freezing). Laird's Distillery (New Jersey, 1698), the oldest operating distillery in the USA.
wiki.map.appletiser.desc: Carbonated apple juice from South Africa (Elgin, 1966). Popular non-alcoholic brunch alternative.
wiki.map.asti.desc: Sweet Piedmontese sparkling wine from Moscato. Low-alcohol, fruity, and floral.
wiki.map.australian-whisky.desc: Tasmania leads the craft scene with Sullivans Cove and Lark. Oceanic air and local barley.
wiki.map.bandol.desc: Mourvèdre-dominant wines on Provence coastal terraces. Characterful reds and saline rosés.
wiki.map.barolo.desc: King of Piedmontese wines. Nebbiolo from Langhe aged at least 38 months.
wiki.map.barossa.desc: Cradle of Australian Shiraz. Vines over 150 years old still producing.
wiki.map.beaujolais.desc: Light reds from Gamay grapes south of Burgundy. Famous for Beaujolais Nouveau on the third Thursday of November.
wiki.map.becherovka.desc: Czech herbal bitter from Karlovy Vary (1807). Considered Czechia's "13th natural spring".
wiki.map.bitter-kas.desc: Basque bitter soft drink inspired by Italian Bitter. A Spanish aperitif classic.
wiki.map.bordeaux.desc: World-reference French wine region. Cabernet Sauvignon and Merlot dominate Médoc and Saint-Émilion.
wiki.map.brunello.desc: Sangiovese Grosso from Montalcino. At least five years of ageing before release.
wiki.map.burgundy.desc: Sacred land of Pinot Noir and Chardonnay. Unique climat system defined by terroir.
wiki.map.canada-dry.desc: Canadian ginger ale created by John McLaughlin in Toronto (1904). Dry and less sweet.
wiki.map.canadian-whisky.desc: Gimli (Manitoba) and other distilleries produce smooth whisky often high in rye. Base of Crown Royal.
wiki.map.cava.desc: Spanish traditional-method sparkling from Penedès. Macabeo, Xarel·lo, and Parellada.
wiki.map.cerveza-belgium.desc: Trappists, lambics, and gueuzes. The world's greatest beer diversity.
wiki.map.cerveza-dublin.desc: Stout capital of the world. Guinness has brewed at St. James's Gate since 1759.
wiki.map.cerveza-munich.desc: Helles, Dunkel, and Weissbier under the 1516 Purity Law. Birthplace of Oktoberfest.
wiki.map.cerveza-pilsner.desc: Pilsen, Czechia: birthplace of golden lager (1842). Global model for clear beer.
wiki.map.cerveza-portland.desc: Epicenter of the American craft revolution. Pacific Northwest hops.
wiki.map.chablis.desc: Mineral, cutting Chardonnay from northern Burgundy. Kimmeridgian soils with marine fossils.
wiki.map.champagne.desc: The only region allowed to use the name. Traditional method with second fermentation in bottle.
wiki.map.cherry-heering.desc: Danish cherry liqueur since 1818. Original ingredient of the Singapore Sling and Blood & Sand.
wiki.map.chianti.desc: Tuscan Sangiovese in the historic straw-covered bottle. Chianti Classico bears the Black Rooster.
wiki.map.chicha-morada.desc: Peruvian drink of purple corn, pineapple, and spices. Sweet, cold, and non-alcoholic, an Inca heritage.
wiki.map.club-mate.desc: German mate soft drink since 1924 (Münchsteinach). Iconic in Berlin's hacker and techno scenes.
wiki.map.coca-cola.desc: Recipe by pharmacist John Pemberton (Atlanta, 1886). The world's most iconic soda.
wiki.map.coffee-brazil.desc: World's largest producer. Minas Gerais concentrates the arabica output.
wiki.map.coffee-colombia.desc: Smooth, balanced Arabica from the Coffee Axis. UNESCO Heritage cultural landscape.
wiki.map.coffee-costa-rica.desc: Arabica-only by law since 1989. Tarrazú and Central Valley yield clean, bright, fruity coffees.
wiki.map.coffee-ethiopia.desc: Cradle of Coffea arabica. Yirgacheffe, Sidamo, and Harrar varieties offer distinct profiles.
wiki.map.coffee-honduras.desc: Copán and Marcala lead Honduras, one of Central America's largest producers. Sweet and balanced.
wiki.map.coffee-jamaica.desc: One of the world's finest and most expensive coffees, grown between 900 and 1700 m.
wiki.map.coffee-kenya.desc: Bright, fruity Arabicas from the highlands. Highly prized in specialty coffee.
wiki.map.coffee-panama.desc: The Geisha variety from Boquete revolutionized specialty coffee in 2004. Record auction prices for its floral-citrus profile.
wiki.map.coffee-sumatra.desc: Mandheling and Gayo grown by the typical Indonesian wet-hulling method. Dense body, earthy and cocoa notes.
wiki.map.coffee-vietnam.desc: Second-largest producer, mostly robusta from the central highlands. Symbol of the cà phê sữa đá with condensed milk.
wiki.map.coffee-yemen.desc: First coffee export port (Mocha, 15th century). Origin of the name mocha.
wiki.map.colchagua.desc: Chilean valley of Cabernet and Carménère, the lost grape of Bordeaux. Mediterranean climate.
wiki.map.cremant.desc: French sparkling wines outside Champagne made by the traditional method: Alsace, Loire, Burgundy, Jura.
wiki.map.creme-de-mure.desc: French liqueur of wild blackberries. Classic in Dick Bradsell's Bramble (1984).
wiki.map.creme-de-peche.desc: French peach liqueur from Savoy. Delicate and fruity.
wiki.map.creme-de-violette.desc: Liqueur made from violet petals. Key ingredient in the classic Aviation.
wiki.map.douro-wines.desc: The Douro yields more than just Port: it also produces powerful dry reds since the Barca Velha revolution (1952). UNESCO landscape.
wiki.map.dr-pepper.desc: The oldest soda in the USA (Waco, 1885). Secret blend of 23 flavors.
wiki.map.english-sparkling.desc: English sparkling wines from Sussex and Kent. Global warming has brought them close to Champagne level.
wiki.map.espresso-italy.desc: Italy invents espresso (Turin, 1884). The culture of caffè al banco.
wiki.map.etna.desc: Volcanic wines from the slopes of Mount Etna, with Nerello Mascalese. Unique minerality and freshness.
wiki.map.falernum.desc: Caribbean spiced syrup with clove, ginger, lime, and almond. Essential in tiki bartending.
wiki.map.fanta.desc: Created in WWII Germany (Essen, 1940) when Coca-Cola could no longer import syrup. Today a global brand with dozens of flavors.
wiki.map.fever-tree.desc: Premium London tonic (2005). Relaunched the culture of quality gin and tonic.
wiki.map.finnish-whisky.desc: Teerenpeli in Lahti has distilled since 2002 with local barley and subarctic lake water.
wiki.map.fireball.desc: Canadian whisky infused with cinnamon (1984). Viral phenomenon of the modern shot.
wiki.map.franciacorta.desc: The Italian Champagne from Lombardy. Chardonnay and Pinot Noir made by the traditional method.
wiki.map.genepi.desc: Alpine liqueur of artemisia (genepì). Tradition of Savoy and the Aosta Valley.
wiki.map.georgia-wines.desc: Cradle of wine (8,000 years). Kakheti keeps vinification in qvevri, buried amphorae — a UNESCO heritage.
wiki.map.gin-menorca.desc: Xoriguer has distilled in Mahón since the 18th century, a British legacy from the island's occupation. DO Gin de Mahón.
wiki.map.ginger-beer-jamaica.desc: Jamaican fermented ginger drink. Base of the Moscow Mule and Dark & Stormy.
wiki.map.guarana.desc: Brazilian soft drink from the Amazonian guaraná berry. Natural caffeine and sweetness.
wiki.map.hermitage.desc: Granite hill of Tain-l'Hermitage (Northern Rhône). Legendary Syrah, long-lived and deep wines.
wiki.map.horchata-valencia.desc: Valencian tiger-nut drink with PDO. Served ice-cold with fartons, a tradition of Alboraya since the 13th century.
wiki.map.inca-kola.desc: Peruvian yellow soda with lemon verbena. Outsells Coca-Cola in Peru.
wiki.map.indian-whisky.desc: Amrut (Bangalore) and Paul John (Goa) prove tropical climate accelerates maturation. Intense, spicy notes.
wiki.map.irn-bru.desc: Fluorescent orange Scottish soda. Scotland's other national drink since 1901.
wiki.map.jura.desc: Small French region of singular wines: oxidative Vin Jaune aged sous voile, like a fino sherry.
wiki.map.kefir.desc: Fermented milk with kefir grains, originally from the Caucasus. The oldest probiotic dairy tradition.
wiki.map.kofola.desc: Czech cola created in 1959 as a socialist alternative to Coca-Cola. Less sweet, flavored with herbs and licorice.
wiki.map.kombucha.desc: SCOBY-fermented tea, originally from Manchuria. Popularized in the West in the 1990s.
wiki.map.kvass.desc: Russian fermented drink made from rye bread. Very low alcohol (<1%), drunk as a summer soft drink.
wiki.map.licor-43.desc: Sweet Spanish liqueur with vanilla and 43 botanicals. Created in Cartagena in 1946.
wiki.map.limoncello.desc: Liqueur from Amalfi, Sorrento, or Capri lemons. Digestif served very cold in frozen glasses.
wiki.map.loire-valley.desc: Sancerre, Vouvray, Muscadet. Aromatic, mineral Chenin Blanc and Sauvignon Blanc.
wiki.map.malta-hatuey.desc: Cuban non-alcoholic malta, a tradition since 1942. Bitter and nutritious, served cold and sometimes with condensed milk.
wiki.map.marlborough.desc: New Zealand Sauvignon Blanc that revolutionized the variety in the 1980s.
wiki.map.mate.desc: South American infusion of Ilex paraguariensis. Shared in a gourd with bombilla.
wiki.map.mendoza.desc: Argentine capital of Malbec at the foot of the Andes. High-altitude wines.
wiki.map.midori.desc: Japanese melon liqueur from Suntory (1978). Neon green color and signature sweetness.
wiki.map.monkey-47.desc: Artisanal Black Forest gin with 47 botanicals, many of them wild. Created in 2010 by a retired Englishman.
wiki.map.moroccan-mint.desc: Gunpowder green tea with spearmint and plenty of sugar, poured from high into small glasses. A Maghreb social ritual.
wiki.map.mosel.desc: German slate-soil Rieslings along the Mosel river. Crystalline acidity.
wiki.map.mountain-dew.desc: Citrus soda from Knoxville (1940), loaded with caffeine. Icon of the American South and gamer culture.
wiki.map.napa.desc: Cradle of Californian wine. Benchmark Cabernet Sauvignon after the Judgment of Paris (1976).
wiki.map.nero-davola.desc: Flagship red grape of Sicily, grown near Avola. Powerful, fruity Mediterranean reds.
wiki.map.orange-bitters.desc: Citrus bitters made from bitter orange peel and spices. Nearly extinct during Prohibition, revived by the modern cocktail revival.
wiki.map.orangina.desc: Born in Algeria (Boufarik, 1936) and relaunched in Marseille. Real orange pulp in its bulbous bottle.
wiki.map.pastis.desc: Anise liqueur from Marseille with green anise and licorice. Drunk with iced water, turning white and cloudy.
wiki.map.pepsi.desc: Created in 1893 by Caleb Bradham in North Carolina. Historic rival of Coca-Cola.
wiki.map.pimms.desc: English gin-based aperitif (1823). Heart of the Pimm's Cup served at Wimbledon.
wiki.map.plymouth-gin.desc: Sweeter style than London Dry, distilled at Black Friars Distillery since 1793. The only gin with geographical protection in the UK.
wiki.map.portland-craft-gin.desc: Oregon led the American craft gin revolution with Aviation, New Deal, and other distilleries from the 2000s.
wiki.map.priorat.desc: Catalan DOCa of mineral reds grown on llicorella slate. Old Garnacha and Cariñena vines.
wiki.map.prosecco.desc: Venetian sparkling from Glera grape. Charmat method in large tanks — fresh and floral.
wiki.map.provence-rose.desc: Cradle of modern French rosé. Grenache, Cinsault, and Mourvèdre yield pale, elegant wines.
wiki.map.pulque.desc: Pre-Hispanic Mexican drink fermented from maguey aguamiel. Sacred to the Aztecs, still alive in the highlands.
wiki.map.ramune.desc: Japanese soda with a Codd marble bottle (1884). Original lemon-lime flavor.
wiki.map.rheingau.desc: Noble Rieslings of the Rhine. Birthplace of Kabinett and Spätlese.
wiki.map.rhone.desc: Powerful reds of Syrah and Grenache. Châteauneuf-du-Pape and Hermitage fly its flag.
wiki.map.rhum-haiti.desc: Barbancourt has distilled fresh-cane rhum agricole since 1862. Double distillation in a Charentais pot still.
wiki.map.rias-baixas.desc: Galician Albariño from the Atlantic rías. Marine salinity and minerality.
wiki.map.ribera-duero.desc: Robust, long-lived Tempranillo from the upper Duero. Home of Vega Sicilia.
wiki.map.rioja.desc: Spain's most prestigious DOCa. Aged Tempranillo: crianza, reserva, gran reserva.
wiki.map.ron-bermudas.desc: Gosling's Black Seal since 1806. Heart of the Dark & Stormy, the island's official cocktail.
wiki.map.ron-mexico.desc: Veracruz, Mexico's sugar-cane state, has produced smooth rums since the colonial era. Mocambo and Prohibido are benchmarks.
wiki.map.ron-nicaragua.desc: Flor de Caña has distilled in Chichigalpa since 1890, next to the San Cristóbal volcano. Rum with no added sugar.
wiki.map.ron-paraguay.desc: Paraguay makes light, white rums — less known abroad but with centuries of tradition.
wiki.map.rooibos.desc: South African infusion of Aspalathus linearis, exclusive to the Cederberg mountains. Caffeine-free, reddish, naturally sweet.
wiki.map.rye-indiana.desc: MGP in Lawrenceburg supplies most of the American rye bottled under independent labels. Backbone of the Manhattan.
wiki.map.sambuca.desc: Italian liqueur of star anise, elderflower, and licorice. Served with three coffee beans (le mosche, "the flies").
wiki.map.santorini.desc: Assyrtiko grown in koulouras (basket-shaped vines) on volcanic soils. One of the world's oldest winemaking traditions.
wiki.map.schweppes.desc: Jacob Schweppe invented commercial carbonated water in Geneva (1783). Father of tonic water.
wiki.map.sekt.desc: German sparkling wine from Riesling and other varieties. Tradition since the 19th century.
wiki.map.sidra-asturias.desc: Natural cider poured from height (escanciada). A millennia-old Celtic tradition.
wiki.map.sidra-normandie.desc: Cider made from bitter Norman apples. Base of Calvados.
wiki.map.slivovitz.desc: Traditional plum brandy from the Balkans. National symbol in Serbia, Bosnia, and Czechia.
wiki.map.sloe-gin.desc: Gin macerated with wild sloes (Prunus spinosa). A rural English tradition.
wiki.map.sonoma.desc: Elegant reds and coastal Chardonnays from California. More diverse and cooler than Napa.
wiki.map.sprite.desc: Clear lemon-lime created by Coca-Cola in 1961 as an answer to 7UP. Atlanta, Georgia.
wiki.map.stellenbosch.desc: South Africa's winemaking heart since 1679. Pinotage is its native grape.
wiki.map.taiwanese-whisky.desc: Kavalan (Yilan, 2005) has burst onto the world stage with rapid maturation from heat and humidity. Internationally awarded.
wiki.map.tea-assam.desc: Robust, malty black tea. Backbone of most English Breakfast blends.
wiki.map.tea-ceylon.desc: Bright, citrusy teas from Sri Lanka grown at different altitudes.
wiki.map.tea-darjeeling.desc: The Champagne of tea on Himalayan slopes. Iconic first flush and second flush.
wiki.map.tea-fujian.desc: Cradle of oolong and red teas (Wuyi Shan). Ancient cliffside cultivations.
wiki.map.tea-taiwan.desc: Floral oolongs from Alishan and Dong Ding. Gongfu cha culture.
wiki.map.tea-uji.desc: Cradle of Japanese matcha and gyokuro. A tradition since the 12th century.
wiki.map.tea-yunnan.desc: Home of fermented pu-erh. Ancient wild tea trees thousands of years old.
wiki.map.thums-up.desc: India's best-selling cola, created in 1977 after Coca-Cola's temporary departure. Bolder flavor than its rivals.
wiki.map.tia-maria.desc: Jamaican liqueur of Blue Mountain coffee and rum. Base of the modern Espresso Martini.
wiki.map.tokaj.desc: Hungarian Aszú from botrytized grapes. Called "the wine of kings, the king of wines" by Louis XIV.
wiki.map.triple-sec.desc: Orange liqueur created by Combier in Saumur (1834). Base of the Margarita, Sidecar, and Cosmopolitan.
wiki.map.turkish-rize.desc: Cultivated in Rize (Black Sea) since 1938. Brewed in a double çaydanlık teapot, served all day in tulip glasses.
wiki.map.txakoli.desc: Light, slightly sparkling Basque white wine. Poured from a height into a short glass.
wiki.map.vimto.desc: Red-fruit and spice concentrate created in Manchester (1908). Hugely popular in the UK and the Arab world during Ramadan.
wiki.map.vinho-verde.desc: Light, lightly sparkling whites from Portugal's Minho. Alvarinho and Loureiro grapes, very fresh and low in alcohol.
wiki.map.vodka-finland.desc: Koskenkorva and Finlandia distill with six-row barley and ultra-pure glacier water. A Nordic benchmark.
wiki.map.vodka-usa.desc: Tito's Handmade Vodka (Austin, 1997) triggered the American craft vodka boom. Corn base.
wiki.map.welsh-whisky.desc: Penderyn revives Welsh whisky (2000) after a century of silence. Distilled in a unique Faraday still.
wiki.map.willamette.desc: Oregon Pinot Noir comparable to Burgundy. Cool climate, ideal for the variety.
wiki.map.zubrowka.desc: Polish vodka flavored with bison grass from the Białowieża forest. A unique herbal flavor.
wiki.art.amaros.jagermeister.sub: The world's most famous German herbal liqueur
wiki.art.amaros.jagermeister.description: Jägermeister ("master hunter" in German) is a German herbal liqueur (35% ABV) made with 56 herbs, fruits, roots, and spices. Created in 1935 in Wolfenbüttel, it is the world's best-selling German digestif and one of the most recognizable liqueurs. While many associate it with party shots and Jägerbombs, it is a sophisticated amaro with a complex recipe that deserves to be taken seriously as both a cocktail ingredient and a digestif.
wiki.art.amaros.jagermeister.history: 1878: Wilhelm Mast founds a vinegar works in Wolfenbüttel. 1935: his son Curt Mast creates Jägermeister. 1960s-1970s: it establishes itself as the standard German digestif. 1980s: Sidney Frank Importing introduces it en masse to the American market as a party shot. 1997: the Jägerbomb (Jägermeister + Red Bull) is invented and becomes a global party phenomenon. 2000s: Jägermeister cold-shot machines appear in bars worldwide. 2010s: the cocktail revival begins to recognize Jägermeister as a legitimate, complex amaro.
wiki.art.amaros.jagermeister.origin: Wolfenbüttel, Lower Saxony, Germany. Curt Mast, son of vinegar-works founder Wilhelm Mast, created the recipe in 1935, inspired by the German tradition of hunter's liqueurs. The logo of a stag with a glowing cross between its antlers represents Saint Hubertus, patron saint of hunters. The original distillery remains in Wolfenbüttel and produces the entire global output.
wiki.art.amaros.jagermeister.production: 56 ingredients: saffron, Ceylon cinnamon, ginger root, star anise, cardamom, bitter orange peel, gentian root, lavender, poppy, red sandalwood, and dozens more herbs, roots, fruits, and barks from around the world. Individual macerates are prepared and rested in oak barrels for 1 year. They are blended, filtered, and bottled at 35% ABV. The entire process takes more than 12 months. Every bottle contains the same globally standardized blend.
wiki.art.amaros.jagermeister.tasting: Aroma: complex herbs, licorice, anise, cinnamon, gentian, dark citrus. Palate: sweet-herbal entry evolving quickly into gentian and root bitterness, warm spices (cinnamon, cardamom), licorice, balsamic notes. Finish: long, bitter-sweet, mentholated, and spiced. Served at -18°C (as the brand recommends), the cold mutes the sweetness and highlights the herbs. Manifest is softer, with oak and vanilla notes.
wiki.art.amaros.jagermeister.tips: Always serve at -18°C — from the freezer or the Tap Machine. At room temperature it loses balance and turns cloying. The Jäger Sour is the best way to showcase Jägermeister as a serious cocktail ingredient. Manifest (premium) is sipped neat at cellar temperature, like an Italian amaro. Don't dismiss the Jägerbomb — it is what it is, but it works. In Germany it is drunk as a digestif after a heavy meal, not as a party shot. Store in the freezer.
wiki.art.amaros.jagermeister.types: Jägermeister Original (35% ABV — the classic, 56 ingredients). Jägermeister Manifest (38% ABV — premium version with additional oak-barrel maturation, smoother and more complex). Jägermeister Cold Brew Coffee (33% ABV — with cold-brew coffee and cocoa, launched 2019). Jägermeister Scharf (33% ABV — with spicy ginger, German market). The Tap Machine chills to -18°C for perfect shots.
wiki.art.amaros.jagermeister.cocktails: Jägerbomb (Jägermeister, Red Bull — the world's most popular shot, simple but effective). Jäger Mule (Jägermeister, ginger beer, lime — the herbal Moscow Mule). Jäger Sour (Jägermeister, lemon, simple syrup, egg white — surprisingly elegant). Deer & Beer (Jägermeister + beer — German tradition). Jäger Old Fashioned (Jägermeister, bourbon, bitters — for cocktail nerds). Jäger Negroni (Jägermeister replaces Campari — a German herbal version).
wiki.art.amaros.orange-bitters.descripti: Orange Bitters are aromatic bitters made on a base of bitter orange (Citrus aurantium), essential in classic pre-Prohibition bartending. They were the Martini and Manhattan's original third ingredient before falling into oblivion during the 20th century. Their 2000s revival returned them to their rightful place: a bridge between bitter and citrus that balances and elevates any cocktail.
wiki.art.amaros.orange-bitters.history: 1862: Jerry Thomas documents orange bitters in his "Bartender's Guide". 1880-1920: ubiquitous in Victorian and Edwardian bartending — present in Martinis, Manhattans, and Gin Fizzes. 1920-1933: Prohibition destroys American cocktail culture. 1960s-1990s: orange bitters all but disappear from the market. 1991: Gary Regan creates Regans' Orange Bitters No. 6, starting the revival. 2007: Angostura launches its own version. Today they are considered the third essential bitters alongside Angostura and Peychaud's.
wiki.art.amaros.orange-bitters.origin: England and the United States, 19th century. Multiple producers created versions: Angostura (Trinidad, 2007), Regans' (Gary Regan, USA, 1991), Fee Brothers (Rochester, NY, 1864). The tradition of orange bitters is as old as cocktails themselves — they appear in recipes from Jerry Thomas's 1862 book.
wiki.art.amaros.orange-bitters.productio: Base of bitter orange peels (Citrus aurantium) macerated in high-proof neutral alcohol. Complementary spices are added: cardamom, coriander, juniper, gentian. Every brand has its own profile: Angostura Orange is more spiced, Regans' more citrus-forward, Fee Brothers sweeter. ABV ranges from 9% (Fee) to 45% (Angostura).
wiki.art.amaros.orange-bitters.tasting: Aroma: intense bitter orange, citrus peel, warm spices (cardamom, coriander). Palate: elegant orange bitterness, not sweet, with depth from gentian and spices. Finish: clean citrus with lingering bitterness. Orange bitters add complexity without dominating — the perfect balancer between sweetness and bitterness in cocktails.
wiki.art.amaros.orange-bitters.tips: 1-2 dashes are enough — they complement, not dominate. Perfect in any gin or vermouth cocktail. Regans' for a pure citrus profile, Angostura Orange for more spiced complexity. Transform a Gin & Tonic by adding 2 dashes. In a Dry Martini, orange bitters is the secret ingredient that sets a professional bartender apart. Store at room temperature; they keep for years.
wiki.art.amaros.orange-bitters.types: Angostura Orange Bitters (28% ABV, spiced and complex). Regans' Orange Bitters No. 6 (45% ABV, pure citrus, a bartender favorite). Fee Brothers West Indian Orange Bitters (9% ABV, sweeter, with glycerin). The Bitter Truth Orange Bitters (39% ABV, European style). Scrappy's Orange Bitters (artisanal, Seattle). Every brand has its own profile — a professional bar should have at least two.
wiki.art.amaros.orange-bitters.cocktails: Dry Martini (gin, dry vermouth, 1-2 dashes orange bitters — the original pre-Prohibition recipe). Bijou (gin, sweet vermouth, Chartreuse, orange bitters). Martinez (Old Tom gin, sweet vermouth, maraschino, orange bitters — the Martini's forerunner). Pegu Club (gin, curaçao, lime, Angostura + orange bitters). Adonis (sweet vermouth, sherry, orange bitters — a spirit-based low-proof cocktail). Old Fashioned variant (bourbon, orange bitters instead of Angostura for a more citrus profile).
wiki.art.amaros.peychauds-bitters.descri: Peychaud's Bitters are aromatic bitters created in New Orleans, fundamental to the Sazerac cocktail and to American cocktail culture. Unlike Angostura (more spiced), Peychaud's has a more floral, fruity profile with anise notes. They are the world's second most important bitters after Angostura and a must-have ingredient in any professional bar.
wiki.art.amaros.peychauds-bitters.histor: 1830s: Antoine Peychaud creates the bitters at his New Orleans pharmacy. 1838: they become popular in the city's coffee houses. 1850s: combined with absinthe and rye whiskey, they create the Sazerac, considered the first American cocktail. 1869: the brand is commercially registered. 2008: Sazerac Company acquires the brand. Peychaud's is declared the "official bitters of New Orleans" and protected as cultural heritage.
wiki.art.amaros.peychauds-bitters.origin: New Orleans, Louisiana, United States.
